options.content: Comparing one business's ratios with another business's
options.rationale: Correct: comparing different businesses for the same period.

options.content: Comparing one business's ratios over several years
options.rationale: That is a trend (comparison over time).

options.content: Comparing budgeted figures with actual figures
options.rationale: That is budgetary control, not inter-business comparison.

options.content: Comparing a trial balance with the ledger accounts
options.rationale: That is part of checking the records.

explanation: Inter-business comparison judges a business against others, ideally in the same trade.

stem: A supermarket has a much faster rate of inventory turnover than a jewellery shop. What is the main reason?

options.content: They are different types of business
options.rationale: Correct: everyday goods sell far faster than jewellery.

options.content: The supermarket uses straight-line depreciation
options.rationale: Depreciation does not affect inventory turnover.

options.content: The jewellery shop has a later year end
options.rationale: A year end might shift inventory a little, but not explain a large gap.

options.content: The supermarket has a higher gross margin
options.rationale: Supermarkets usually have lower margins.

explanation: Ratios differ naturally between trades; compare like with like.

stem: Two identical shops use different depreciation methods. Shop P's depreciation charge is higher. Compared with Shop Q, Shop P will show …

options.content: a lower gross profit margin
options.rationale: Depreciation is below gross profit.

options.content: a higher ROCE
options.rationale: Lower profit usually means a lower ROCE.

options.content: a lower profit margin
options.rationale: Correct: higher depreciation means lower profit for the same revenue.

options.content: a higher current ratio
options.rationale: Depreciation does not affect current assets or liabilities.

explanation: A different accounting policy changes the profit figure even though trading is the same.

stem: Business X bought all its equipment ten years ago; Business Y bought identical equipment last year. Both earn the same profit. Why is X's ROCE likely to be higher?

options.content: X charges more depreciation every year
options.rationale: Older assets usually carry less depreciation, not more, and profits are equal here.

options.content: X has a higher gross profit margin than Y
options.rationale: The question says profits are the same.

options.content: X has a lower current ratio than Y
options.rationale: The current ratio does not affect ROCE.

options.content: Its capital employed is lower
options.rationale: Correct: its old assets are heavily depreciated, so the same profit is divided by a smaller figure.

explanation: Old assets at a low net book value reduce capital employed, flattering ROCE.
hints: ROCE = profit before interest ÷ capital employed.

stem: Which is a **problem** of comparing two businesses using only their latest statements?

options.content: Ratios turn figures into percentages
options.rationale: This is what makes comparison possible.

options.content: One year may be unusual for either business
options.rationale: Correct: a single year may not show the normal position.

options.content: Both businesses use the same year end
options.rationale: This makes comparison easier, not harder.

options.content: Both businesses sell similar goods
options.rationale: This also makes comparison fairer.

explanation: Trends over several years are more reliable than one year's figures.

stem: Shop M's year ends on 31 December, just after the festive season; Shop N's ends on 30 November. Which ratio is most likely to be distorted by the different dates?

options.content: The mark-up
options.rationale: The mark-up depends on prices, which the date does not change.

options.content: The gross profit margin
options.rationale: Margins over a whole year are not much affected by the closing date.

options.content: The acid test ratio
options.rationale: Correct: inventory and cash on the two dates differ sharply.

options.content: The profit margin
options.rationale: This is a whole-year figure.

explanation: Ratios built from statement of financial position figures (inventory, cash, payables) depend on the date; shops hold far more stock before a busy season.
hints: Which ratios use figures from one date rather than the whole year?

stem: A large wholesaler has a higher gross profit margin than a small retailer selling similar goods. Which factor most likely explains this?

options.content: Lower rent for its premises
options.rationale: Rent is an expense below gross profit.

options.content: A longer credit period for customers
options.rationale: Credit terms do not change the margin.

options.content: Smaller loans and less interest
options.rationale: Interest is below gross profit.

options.content: Bulk buying at lower unit cost
options.rationale: Correct: size brings bigger purchase discounts.

explanation: Economies of scale in buying raise gross profit for the same selling prices.

stem: An investor wants to compare two hardware shops fairly. Which step would make the comparison **most** reliable?

options.content: Compare the shops' revenue in dollars only
options.rationale: Size differences make raw dollar figures misleading.

options.content: Use several years of figures for both shops
options.rationale: Correct: trends reduce the effect of one unusual year.

options.content: Use only the shop with the higher profit
options.rationale: Comparison needs both businesses.

options.content: Ignore their accounting policies
options.rationale: Different policies must be checked, not ignored.

explanation: Several years of data, similar policies and similar businesses all improve comparability.
hints: Think about the problems of comparison and which one this removes.

stem: If two businesses use different methods of depreciation, their profit figures may differ even though they trade identically.
explanation: True. Accounting policies affect reported profit and asset values.

stem: A higher gross profit margin always shows that a business is better managed than another.
explanation: False. Margins depend on the type of business and strategy; a low-margin, high-volume business can be very successful.

stem: Match each situation with the factor that explains why the two businesses' ratios differ.

left.content: A bakery and a car dealer have very different inventory turnover
A chain buys in bulk and gets bigger discounts than a corner shop
One shop uses reducing balance depreciation, the other straight line
One business pays loan interest, the other is funded by the owner
A shop in central Harare pays far higher rent than one in a small town

explanation: Each situation is a typical reason why ratios differ between businesses.
hints: Ask what is really different about the two businesses in each case.

payload.template: Comparisons between businesses are most useful when the businesses are of the same {{blank:a}}, use the same {{blank:b}} policies and prepare statements to the same {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Like-for-like comparison needs similar businesses, policies and year ends.

stem: Shop A had revenue of US\$145,000 and gross profit of US\$43,500. Shop B had revenue of US\$88,000 and gross profit of US\$30,800. By how many percentage points is Shop B's gross profit margin higher than Shop A's? Give your answer to one decimal place.

Two identical shops each have revenue of US\$160,000, gross profit of US\$52,000 and other expenses (excluding depreciation) of US\$30,500, and no loans. Shop C charges depreciation of US\$3,000 and has capital employed of US\$90,000. Shop D charges depreciation of US\$7,500, so its capital employed is US\$85,500. Calculate Shop D's ROCE, to one decimal place.
explanation: Shop D profit = 52,000 − 30,500 − 7,500 = 14,000. ROCE = 14,000 ÷ 85,500 × 100 = 16.4% (Shop C: 20.6%). Using Shop C's capital employed gives 15.6%.
workedSolution: 1. Shop D profit = 52,000 − 30,500 − 7,500 = 14,000. ROCE = 14,000 ÷ 85,500 × 100 = 16.4% (Shop C: 20.6%). Using Shop C's capital employed gives 15.6%.
hints: Profit = gross profit − other expenses − depreciation.

stem: A hardware shop's cost of sales was US\$54,000; inventory was US\$5,600 at the start and US\$6,400 at the end of the year. The average rate of inventory turnover for hardware shops in the area is 6.5 times. Calculate the shop's rate of inventory turnover, to one decimal place.
explanation: Average inventory 6,000; 54,000 ÷ 6,000 = 9.0 times, faster than the local average of 6.5.
workedSolution: 1. Average inventory 6,000; 54,000 ÷ 6,000 = 9.0 times, faster than the local average of 6.5.

stem: State **two** factors, other than accounting policies, that may cause the ratios of two businesses to differ.

points.description: Size / location / method of financing / age of non-current assets / business strategy

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The two businesses may sell different types of goods, and one may be much larger and able to buy in bulk.

stem: Tendai's ROCE is 14%; his competitor's is 21%. Tendai's equipment is new; his competitor's is nine years old. Evaluate whether Tendai's business is performing worse.

points.description: Competitor's old equipment has a low net book value, so its capital employed is low and ROCE is flattered
Tendai's new assets raise capital employed and depreciation, lowering his ROCE
Conclusion: the gap may not mean worse performance; compare other ratios / several years / note competitor may soon need to replace equipment

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Not necessarily. The competitor's equipment is almost fully depreciated, so its capital employed is small and its ROCE looks high. Tendai's new equipment increases both his capital employed and his depreciation. The competitor will soon face replacement costs, so Tendai should compare margins and several years' results before concluding he is doing worse.

explanation: Asset age is a key factor in comparing ROCE.
hints: Think about how asset age affects capital employed.

stem:
Rudo has savings to invest and is considering two hardware businesses in Gweru. Their figures for 2025:

|  | Tatenda Traders US\$ | Sipho Stores US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue | 210,000 | 132,000 |
| Cost of sales | 155,400 | 85,800 |
| Expenses (including any loan interest) | 31,500 | 33,360 |
| Loan interest included in expenses | – | 2,400 |
| Capital employed | 120,000 | 95,000 |
| Current assets (including inventory) | 33,600 | 18,900 |
| Inventory | 21,000 | 12,600 |
| Current liabilities | 16,800 | 12,600 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate Sipho Stores' gross profit margin, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate Sipho Stores' return on capital employed, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate Sipho Stores' acid test ratio, as x : 1 to two decimal places.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State **two** problems Rudo may face in comparing the two businesses.

points.description: Different accounting policies, year ends, only one year's figures, or different financing (Sipho has a loan)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Tatenda Traders is much larger, so it may buy in bulk; and the businesses may use different depreciation policies, so their profits are not calculated in the same way.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Advise Rudo which business appears the better investment. Justify your answer using the ratios.

points.description: Sipho Stores has the higher gross margin (35.0% v 26.0%)
Tatenda Traders has the higher ROCE (19.3% v 16.0%) and better liquidity (acid test 0.75 v 0.50 : 1)
Conclusion with justification, e.g. Tatenda Traders, because return on capital and liquidity matter most to an investor (or reasoned alternative)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Sipho Stores earns a higher gross margin (35.0% against 26.0%), but its expenses and loan interest are high, so its ROCE is only 16.0% compared with 19.3% for Tatenda Traders. Tatenda Traders is also more liquid (acid test 0.75 : 1 against 0.50 : 1). Rudo should prefer Tatenda Traders, after checking that both use similar accounting policies.

parts.explanation: A justified recommendation using at least two ratios.

explanation: Tatenda Traders: GPM 26.0%, ROCE 19.3%, acid test 0.75 : 1. Sipho Stores: GPM 35.0%, ROCE 16.0%, acid test 0.50 : 1.
hints: Acid test = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities.

stem: Nyasha and Farai each opened a stationery shop on 1 January 2025 with equipment costing US\$32,000. In 2025 both shops made gross profit of US\$48,000 and had other expenses of US\$27,200. Nyasha depreciates equipment at 12.5% per annum straight line; Farai uses 30% per annum reducing balance.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why a comparison of the two shops' profit margins could mislead an investor, and what the investor should do.

points.description: The difference of 5,600 is caused only by the depreciation policy, not by trading
So Farai's profit margin looks lower although the businesses performed equally
Investor should adjust to the same policy / compare gross margins / check accounting policies before comparing

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Both shops traded identically; Farai's profit is US\$5,600 lower only because he charges more depreciation in the first year. His profit margin therefore looks worse. An investor should restate both on the same depreciation policy, or compare gross margins, before judging them.

hints: Reducing balance in year 1 = rate × cost.
